# Complex Projective Plane and Cross Ratio

## Projective Plane
::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
Given sets $\mathbb{P}$ and $\mathbb{L}$, the elements in $\mathbb{P}$ are called **points**, and the elements in $\mathbb{L}$ are called **lines**. Given a subset $\mathcal{I}$ of the set $\mathbb{P}\times \mathbb{L}$, then for a point $P$, define 
$$
\mathbb{L}_P=\{\ell\in \mathbb{L}\mid (P,\ell)\in \mathcal{I}\}
$$
for a line $\ell$, define 
$$
\mathbb{P}_{\ell}=\{P\in \mathbb{P}\mid (P,\ell)\in \mathcal{I}\}
$$
If $\mathcal{P}=(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{L},\mathcal{I})$ satisfies

(1) For all points $P$, $|\mathbb{L}_P|>1$; for all lines $\ell$, $|\mathbb{P}_\ell|>1$.

(2) For two distinct lines $\ell_1,\ell_2$, there exists a unique point $P\in\mathbb{P}_{\ell_1}\cap \mathbb{P}_{\ell_2}$. We write $P=\ell_1\cap \ell_2$.

(3) For two distinct points $P_1,P_2$, there exists a unique line $\ell\in \mathbb{L}_{P_1}\cap \mathbb{L}_{P_2}$. We write $\ell=P_1P_2$.

then $\mathcal{P}$ is a **projective plane**.
:::

Suppose that points $P_1,P_2$ satisfy $\mathbb{L}_{P_1}=\mathbb{L}_{P_2}$, then $|\mathbb{L}_{P_1}\cap \mathbb{L}_{P_2}|>1$, i.e. $P_1=P_2$. In other words, we may identify $P$ with $\mathbb{L}_P$, and similarly, we may identify $\ell$ and $\mathbb{P}_{\ell}$. Since $(P,\ell)\in \mathcal{I}$ and $P\in \mathbb{P}_{\ell}$ are equivalent, we may also write $P\in \ell$ (or $\ell\in P$, but this is rarely used), and say that $P$ is on $\ell$, or $\ell$ passes through $P$.

If some points are on the same line, then they are said to be **collinear**; and if some lines pass through the same point, then they are said to be **concurrent**.

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Remark.**
Under the usual framework, a projective plane is the set of points, i.e. the set $\mathbb{P}$, and define lines to be some specific subsets of $\mathbb{P}$, i.e. $\mathbb{P}_\ell$. This is the reason why the notation $\ell\in P$ is rarely used. To emphasize that the roles of the points and lines are interchangeable (i.e. duality), we used $\mathcal{I}$ (incidence set) to encode the relations of points and lines. In this way, there is no specific hierarchy between points and lines.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Example.**
Let $\mathbb{P}=\{P_1,P_2,\ldots,P_7\}$, and $\mathbb{L}=\{\ell_1,\ell_2,\ldots,\ell_7\}$, and define
$$
P_i\in \ell_j\iff j-i\equiv 1,2,4\pmod 7
$$
i.e. $\mathcal{I}=\{(P_i,\ell_j)\mid j-i\equiv 1,2,4\pmod 7\}$. In this case, $\mathcal{P}=(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{L},\mathcal{I})$ is a projective plane, and there are three points (resp. lines) on each line (resp. point).
:::

## Cross Ratio 
::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
On a projective plane, for any collinear points $P_1,P_2,Q_1,Q_2$, satisfying $P_i\neq Q_j$ ($i,j\neq 1,2$), define the cross ratio $$(P_1,P_2;Q_1,Q_2)\in \mathbb{C}-\{0\}=\mathbb{C}^\times$$ of the four points to be a function satisfying the following hypothesis.

(1) $(P_1,P_2;Q_1,Q_2)=(Q_1,Q_2;P_1,P_2)$.

(2) If $P_3$ and $Q_1,Q_2$ are distinct, then 
$$
(P_1,P_2;Q_1,Q_2)=(P_1,P_3;Q_1,Q_2)\cdot (P_3,P_2;Q_1,Q_2)
$$

(3) Given point $P$ and lines $m,n$ satisfying $P\notin m,n$, then for distinct $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3,\ell_4\in \mathbb{L}_P$, 
$$
(\ell_1\cap m,\ell_2\cap m;\ell_3\cap m,\ell_4\cap m)=(\ell_1\cap n,\ell_2\cap n;\ell_3\cap n,\ell_4\cap n)
$$

(4) Given line $\ell$ and distinct points $P_1,P_2,P_3\in \ell$, then for any $c\in \mathbb{C}^\times$, there exists a unique $P\in \ell$ such that $(P_1,P_2;P_3,P)=c$ ($P\neq P_1,P_2$).

A projective space equipped with a cross ratio is called a complex projective plane.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Consider the resultant of the defining homogeneous polynomials $F$ and $G$:
$$
\operatorname{Res}(F, G) = 0
$$
Thus the intersection is non-empty. $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {#rem-coord}
## Homogeneous Coordinates
Note that $(X:Y:Z)$ are defined up to a non-zero scalar multiple.
:::

As shown in @rem-coord, intersection multiplicities are well-defined.
